sampling-dist-mean-s1.title: Drive-through wait times
sampling-dist-mean-s1.text: A coffee chain records the wait time of every car at its drive-through windows (invented data). Over many thousands of cars, the wait times have mean $\mu = 4.2$ minutes and standard deviation $\sigma = 2.8$ minutes, and their distribution is strongly skewed right. A manager takes a random sample of 40 cars from last month and computes the sample mean wait time $\bar{x}$.

table.caption: The population of wait times and the sample

sampling-dist-mean-s2.title: Simulated means of 16 bags of chips
sampling-dist-mean-s2.text: A snack company fills bags whose weights are normally distributed with mean $\mu = 28.4$ grams and standard deviation $\sigma = 1.2$ grams. A quality team simulated 40 random samples of 16 bags each and recorded each sample mean $\bar{x}$ (invented data). The dotplot shows the 40 sample means.

plot.label: Dotplot of 40 simulated sample means of 16 bag weights, centered near 28.4 grams and ranging from about 27.8 to 29.0 grams

items.q: What are the mean and the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ for samples of 40 cars?
options: Mean 4.2 minutes, standard deviation about 0.44 minutes
Mean 4.2 minutes, standard deviation 2.8 minutes
Mean 4.2 minutes, standard deviation 0.07 minutes
Mean 0.44 minutes, standard deviation 2.8 minutes
The mean of $\bar{x}$ equals $\mu = 4.2$, and its standard deviation is $\frac{2.8}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 0.44$ minutes.
2.8 minutes is the spread of single wait times. Averages of 40 cars vary much less: divide by $\sqrt{40}$.
That divides 2.8 by 40. The standard deviation of $\bar{x}$ divides by the square root of $n$, not by $n$.
The center does not shrink. The sample mean is an unbiased estimator, so its mean is $\mu = 4.2$.

items.q: The wait times are strongly skewed. Why is a normal model still reasonable for the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$?
options: The population of wait times is approximately normal
40 cars is less than 10% of the cars served
The sample size of 40 is at least 30, so the central limit theorem applies
The cars were chosen at random from last month

why.correct: The central limit theorem: for a random sample with $n \ge 30$, the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal even when the population is skewed.
options: The stimulus says the population is strongly skewed right. The normal shape comes from the large sample, not the population.
The 10% condition justifies the standard deviation formula. It says nothing about shape.
With $n = 40 \ge 30$, the central limit theorem says the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal whatever the population shape.
Random selection is needed, but it does not by itself make the shape normal. The sample size does that.

items.q: Write the expression for the z-score of a sample mean of 5 minutes in the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$. Type it as you would on the exam, for example (a - b)/(c/sqrt(n)).

why.correct: $z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} = \frac{5 - 4.2}{2.8/\sqrt{40}} = 1.81$. The standard deviation in the denominator is the one for $\bar{x}$, not for single cars.

mistakes.why: That uses the standard deviation of single wait times. A sample mean of 40 cars has standard deviation 2.8 divided by sqrt(40).
Divide by the square root of the sample size, sqrt(40), not by 40.

items.q: What is the probability that the mean wait time of the 40 sampled cars is more than 5 minutes?

why.correct: The sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal with mean 4.2 and standard deviation $\frac{2.8}{\sqrt{40}} = 0.443$. $P(\bar{x} > 5) = P\left(z > \frac{5 - 4.2}{0.443}\right) = P(z > 1.81) = 0.035$.

mistakes.why: That uses $\sigma = 2.8$, the spread of single cars. For a mean of 40 cars use $\frac{2.8}{\sqrt{40}} = 0.443$.
That is the area below 5 minutes. The question asks for more than 5, the upper tail.

items.q: What does checking that 40 is less than 10% of all cars served last month allow the manager to do?
options: Use a normal model for single wait times
Use $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ for the standard deviation of $\bar{x}$
Treat the sample as random
Conclude that the sample mean equals 4.2

why.correct: The 10% condition is about independence when sampling without replacement, so it justifies the standard deviation formula $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$.
options: Single wait times are strongly skewed; no condition changes that.
Sampling without replacement makes the cars slightly dependent. When the sample is under 10% of the population, the formula $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is still accurate.
Randomness comes from how the cars were chosen, not from the sample being a small part of the population.
The sample mean varies from sample to sample; its mean is 4.2, but one sample mean is rarely exactly 4.2.

items.q: The standard deviation of the 40 simulated means is close to which value?
options: 1.2 grams
0.3 grams
0.075 grams
4.8 grams

why.correct: $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.2}{\sqrt{16}} = 0.3$ grams. The simulated means have standard deviation 0.30, as predicted.
options: 1.2 grams is the spread of single bags. The dotplot shows means of 16 bags, which vary less.
The formula gives $\frac{1.2}{\sqrt{16}} = 0.3$ grams, and the dots spread about that much (their standard deviation is 0.30).
That is $\frac{1.2}{16}$: it divides by $n$ instead of $\sqrt{n}$, and it is far narrower than the dots.
That multiplies by $\sqrt{16}$. Averaging makes the spread smaller, not larger.

items.q: The samples have only 16 bags. Why is the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ still normal?
options: 16 is close enough to 30
The dotplot has 40 dots, which is at least 30
Sample means are normal for any population and any sample size
The bag weights themselves are normally distributed

why.correct: A normal population gives a normal sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ at every sample size; the central limit theorem is needed only when the population is not normal.
options: There is no "close enough" rule. The reason here is the normal population.
The 40 dots are 40 samples. The sample size that matters is 16 bags per sample.
For a skewed population and a small sample, $\bar{x}$ keeps some of the skew.
When the population is normal, the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is normal for any sample size.

items.q: Using the normal model for $\bar{x}$, what is the probability that a random sample of 16 bags has a mean weight below 28.0 grams?

why.correct: $\bar{x}$ is normal with mean 28.4 and standard deviation $\frac{1.2}{\sqrt{16}} = 0.3$. $P(\bar{x} < 28.0) = P\left(z < \frac{28.0 - 28.4}{0.3}\right) = P(z < -1.33) = 0.091$. In the dotplot, 5 of the 40 simulated means (0.125) are below 28.0, close to the model value for so few simulated samples.

mistakes.why: That uses $\sigma = 1.2$ for single bags. A mean of 16 bags has standard deviation $\frac{1.2}{\sqrt{16}} = 0.3$.
That is the area above 28.0. "Below 28.0" is the lower tail.

items.q: If the team had used samples of 64 bags instead of 16, how would the spread of the simulated means change?
options: It would be about half as large
It would be about one fourth as large
It would stay about the same
It would be about twice as large
Four times the sample size divides the standard deviation by $\sqrt{4} = 2$: $\frac{1.2}{\sqrt{64}} = 0.15$ grams.
The spread shrinks with the square root of $n$, so four times the bags halves it.
Larger samples give means that vary less, so the dots would bunch closer to 28.4.
More bags in each sample make each mean more precise, so the spread gets smaller.

items.q: For random samples of size $n$ from any population with mean $\mu$, what is the mean of the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$?
options: $\mu$
$\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{n}}$
$\mu$ when $n \ge 30$, and less than $\mu$ otherwise
$n\mu$

why.correct: $\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu$ for every sample size, so $\bar{x}$ is an unbiased estimator of $\mu$.
options: The sample mean is an unbiased estimator: on average over many samples it equals $\mu$.
Dividing by $\sqrt{n}$ applies to the standard deviation, not to the center.
Sample size changes the shape and spread, not the center.
That is the mean of a sum of $n$ values, not of their average.

items.q: Incomes in a town are strongly skewed right. A researcher takes a random sample of 8 households. What shape does the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ have?
options: Approximately normal, because sample means are normal
Skewed left, the opposite of the population
Skewed right, though less skewed than the incomes
Exactly as skewed as the incomes

why.correct: For a skewed population and a small sample, the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is skewed in the same direction, less strongly. A normal model would need $n \ge 30$.
options: Sample means become approximately normal only for a normal population or a large sample.
Averaging pulls the shape toward normal; it does not flip the direction of skew.
With $n = 8$ the central limit theorem cannot be counted on, so some of the population's right skew remains.
Averaging 8 values already reduces the skew, though not enough to call the shape normal.

items.q: A random sample of 50 is taken from a large, strongly skewed population with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ has mean $\mu$
The sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ has standard deviation $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{50}}$
The sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal
The 50 values in the sample are approximately normal
The standard deviation of $\bar{x}$ is $\sigma$
The sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is skewed right, like the population

why.correct: Center $\mu$, spread $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ and an approximately normal shape describe the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$, not the sample itself.
options: Right: $\bar{x}$ is unbiased for $\mu$.
Right: the population is large, so the 10% condition holds.
Right: $n = 50 \ge 30$, so the central limit theorem applies.
The sample looks like the population, so it is skewed too. The central limit theorem is about the means of many samples.
Averages vary less than single values; divide $\sigma$ by $\sqrt{50}$.
With 50 values in each mean, the skew is smoothed away; the central limit theorem gives an approximately normal shape.

items.q: The life of a phone battery is normally distributed with mean 12.5 hours and standard deviation 1.6 hours. What is the probability that the mean life of a random sample of 10 batteries is more than 13 hours?

why.correct: $\bar{x}$ is normal (the population is normal) with mean 12.5 and standard deviation $\frac{1.6}{\sqrt{10}} = 0.506$. $P(\bar{x} > 13) = P\left(z > \frac{13 - 12.5}{0.506}\right) = P(z > 0.99) = 0.162$.

mistakes.why: That is the probability for one battery, using $\sigma = 1.6$. For a mean of 10 batteries use $\frac{1.6}{\sqrt{10}}$.
That is the lower tail, the probability of a mean below 13 hours.

items.q: For the batteries above (mean 12.5 hours, standard deviation 1.6 hours, normal), which is more likely: one battery lasting more than 13 hours, or the mean of 10 batteries being more than 13 hours?
options: The mean of 10 batteries being more than 13 hours
One battery lasting more than 13 hours
They are equally likely, since both have mean 12.5
It depends on whether 10 is at least 30

why.correct: One battery: $z = \frac{13 - 12.5}{1.6} = 0.31$, probability 0.38. A mean of 10: $z = \frac{13 - 12.5}{0.506} = 0.99$, probability 0.16.
options: A mean of 10 stays closer to 12.5, so going past 13 is less likely for the mean.
Single batteries vary more, so a value 0.5 hours above the mean is less unusual for one battery (about 0.38) than for a mean of 10 (about 0.16).
The centers match, but the spreads differ, and spread decides how likely 13 is.
The population is normal, so the sampling distribution is normal; the comparison is about spread.

items.q: A landlord picks a random sample of 60 apartments from the 400 in a complex, without replacement, to estimate the mean monthly water use. What is the problem with using $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{60}}$ as the standard deviation of $\bar{x}$?
options: 60 is more than 10% of 400, so the formula overstates the spread
60 is too small for the central limit theorem
The formula needs the sample standard deviation
Water use is not normally distributed

why.correct: $0.10 \times 400 = 40$ and $60 > 40$. Without replacement, a large share of the population makes the values dependent, and $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is too large.
options: The sample is 15% of the population, so the 10% condition fails and $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is not accurate (the true spread is smaller).
60 is at least 30. The issue is the share of the population sampled.
The formula uses $\sigma$; the problem is independence, not which standard deviation.
With $n = 60$ the shape is fine. The 10% condition is the one that fails.

items.q: Scores on a reading test have population standard deviation $\sigma = 15$ points. What is the standard deviation of the sample mean for random samples of 25 students from a large school district?

why.correct: $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{15}{\sqrt{25}} = \frac{15}{5} = 3$ points. The district is large, so the 10% condition holds.

mistakes.why: That divides 15 by 25. Divide by the square root of the sample size: $\sqrt{25} = 5$.
That is the spread of single scores. Means of 25 students vary less.
